name: Ivan Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Ivan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for the power company in the mountains, on the lines that run over passes and down into the ski villages. A lot of the towers up there you can't drive to, so some days a helicopter flies us in and lowers material on a long line, and we hang off the side of a tower at two thousand metres. Other days it's ordinary work in the valley, new services, a pole hit by an avalanche. I love the mountain jobs, the quiet up there. What wears me out is waiting for weather, sitting in the truck for six hours because the helicopter can't fly.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I hear you're also the one experimenting with new tools on the crew. What does that look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use AI every day, for weather planning, checking load calculations, even for writing my sermons when I preach at our little church, though I rewrite most of it. Last year I talked the company into letting me trial a heavy-lift drone for carrying small loads to towers instead of the helicopter, and it worked well. I like trying new things early, it's how you stay ahead. My wife Hanna does bookkeeping for shops in the village, and with two kids, a mortgage and mountain prices, we don't save much. We spent our cushion on a used truck last spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's a pity, but the tools are still worth using. People who wrote it off will be glad, but I'd keep using what works. I'd probably post that we should judge tools by results, not headlines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit disappointed. I had ideas, like a small business with drones. But my job's secure and my family's fine, so I can't complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and keep using the tools. I'd still push the company to use drones for small loads, because it saves helicopter money. Maybe I'd look into starting a small drone business on the side anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little restless, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you write sermons with AI. How does your congregation feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I haven't told most of them. I use it to organise my thoughts, then I rewrite it in my own words and pray over it. The pastor knows and he's fine with it. The words still have to come from the heart, or they mean nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the drone business look like if you started it anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Inspection jobs for the ski lifts and the private cable cars, maybe deliveries to mountain huts. Small at first, weekends. The trouble is the money, a good drone costs as much as a used car, and we just spent our savings on a truck. I'd have to save up first.

S0.say: I'd say it's a pity but the tools are still worth using, and I'd keep using what works. I'd post that tools should be judged by results, not headlines.
S0.think: I'd be a bit disappointed because I had ideas like a drone business. But my job is secure and my family is fine, so I can't complain.
S0.do: Keeps doing the job and using AI tools, and pushes the company to use drones for small loads to save helicopter costs. Considers starting a small drone business on the side once he has saved.
S0.quote: The words still have to come from the heart, or they mean nothing.
S0.fieldNote: Ivan is curious, entrepreneurial and faithful, combining daily AI use with preaching at his church. He's mildly disappointed by a plateau because it limits his business ideas. Thin savings, recently spent on a truck, hold back his plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for people who are willing to work and learn. Some jobs go, but new ones come, and a man who adapts will do fine. I'd say government should stay out of the way and let businesses and workers figure it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. I already use the tools, and the company will need someone who knows drones and robots in the mountains. I could see myself running a small team doing the technical work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company to make me the lead on drone and robot trials, with a pay rise. I'd save up for my own drone and start doing weekend inspections for the ski lifts. And I'd take every course on grid automation I could find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said government should stay out of the way. What about workers who can't adapt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Families and churches should help them, and businesses should train them. My old mentor, Franz, he's sixty, he'd struggle with the new stuff. I'd help him myself. I don't think a government office in the capital knows Franz better than I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Hanna think about you starting a business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be nervous, she's the one who does the sums. She'd say we can't afford risks with two kids. I'd show her a plan, small steps, no big loans. She'd probably say yes if I promised not to touch the mortgage money.

S1.say: I'd call it a chance for people willing to work and learn, since a man who adapts will do fine. Government should stay out of the way and let businesses and workers work it out.
S1.think: I think it's good for me, because I already use the tools and the company will need a drone and robot person in the mountains. I could see myself running a small technical team.
S1.do: Asks to lead the company's drone and robot trials with a pay rise and saves for his own drone to do weekend ski lift inspections. Takes every grid automation course he can find.
S1.quote: I don't think a government office in the capital knows Franz better than I do.
S1.fieldNote: He sees steady change as an opportunity and would move first, both inside the company and on the side. His free-market, family-and-church outlook shapes how he'd help older colleagues like Franz. His wife's caution acts as a brake on his risk-taking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge shock, but there are opportunities for those who move fast. I'd say people shouldn't wait for government, they should look for where they fit. And I'd say families need to stick together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, two years worries me. We've got almost no savings, and Hanna's bookkeeping would go too, the AI already does half of it. My best shot is to get into the robot side early, maybe working for whoever brings the robots to the mountains, or running a few myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the robot companies right away and offer myself as a mountain specialist, someone who knows the terrain and the weather. I'd try to get a small business loan to buy a couple of drones and offer services to the ski resorts. We'd cut spending to the minimum, no ski passes, no holidays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited about the chance, scared about the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A business loan with almost no savings, during a huge shock. Would a bank lend to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not, that's the honest answer. I'd try the local bank, they know me. If not, maybe my brother-in-law would invest a bit, he has a hardware store. I'd rather owe family than a bank anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Elias and Greta?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them things are changing fast and Dad's going to try something new. Elias is thirteen and loves the drones, he'd want to help. Greta would ask if we can still keep the dog. I'd tell them we'd be fine, and I'd pray that was true.

S2.say: I'd call it a huge shock with opportunities for those who move fast, and say people shouldn't wait for government but find where they fit. Families need to stick together.
S2.think: Two years worries me, because we have almost no savings and my wife's bookkeeping would go too. My best shot is the robot side, working for whoever brings robots to the mountains or running a few myself.
S2.do: Offers himself to robot companies as a mountain specialist and tries for a small loan, from the bank or his brother-in-law, to buy drones for ski resort services. Cuts spending to the minimum, dropping ski passes and holidays.
S2.feel: Anxious, excited about the chance but scared about the money.
S2.quote: Greta would ask if we can still keep the dog.
S2.fieldNote: Even in the fastest scenario he looks for opportunity, but he's honest that a bank may not lend to him. His wife's job is also exposed, which sharpens the money fear. He'd turn to family before government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good chance to get ahead if you're willing to work. I'd tell people to learn the new tools now and plan for what comes. Government shouldn't try to stop it, just make sure people can train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is better. I could save, buy my own drones, build up a small business, and get in early with the robots. It's still a risk, but I'd be on the right side of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save hard for the first year and buy a good heavy-lift drone. I'd start a weekend business doing inspections and small deliveries in the mountains. By year three, I'd look at buying or leasing a robot for line work and offering services to the power company as a contractor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd go from being an employee to selling services to your own company. How would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strange, maybe. But it's how things are going. If the company is going to buy robot services, better from me than from some big firm from the city. I know the mountains, and I'd hire a couple of the lads from my crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different compared with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, I'm scrambling and probably borrowing. With five, I can save, build slowly, and be ready when the robots come. Instead of being run over by the robots, I'd be the one driving them.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a good chance to get ahead if you're willing to work, so people should learn the new tools now. Government shouldn't try to stop it, just make sure people can train.
S3.think: Five years is better, because I could save, buy drones, build a small business and get in early with the robots. It's still a risk, but I'd be on the right side of it.
S3.do: Saves hard in the first year to buy a heavy-lift drone and starts a weekend inspection and delivery business in the mountains. By year three, leases a line-work robot and offers services to the power company as a contractor, hiring lads from his crew.
S3.quote: Instead of being run over by the robots, I'd be the one driving them.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets him plan a move from employee to contractor running his own robots. His loyalty to his crew shows in wanting to hire them. He sees himself on the winning side of the change if he can build slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for people who are ready to work. Plenty of time to train, save and build. I'd say it's a good time to start a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years looks good to me. I could build a proper business with drones and robots, maybe employ a few people from the village. The kids would be grown, and I'd be fifty-three with something of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save and buy drones in the first couple of years, build up the weekend business, and go full-time by year five. I'd lease robots for line work as they become available and offer contracts to the power company. I'd help my kids pick studies that fit the new world, maybe engineering for Elias.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even hopeful. It feels like a real opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you worry that AGI could also run the business, not just the line work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sometimes. If the AI can do everything, maybe it can run a business too. But people still want to deal with someone they know and trust, especially in a village. I'd be the man they call, and the robots would be my crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the ten-year picture that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That my friends on the crew won't move in time. Ten years is long enough that people wait. I'd try to bring as many as I could with me. A business is only as good as its people, even if half of them are robots.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift for people ready to work, with plenty of time to train, save and build. It's a good time to start a business.
S4.think: Ten years looks good, because I could build a proper drone and robot business and maybe employ people from the village. I'd be fifty-three with grown kids and something of my own.
S4.do: Saves and buys drones in the first couple of years and grows the weekend business to full-time by year five. Leases line-work robots as they become available to contract with the power company, and helps his children choose studies like engineering.
S4.feel: Calm and hopeful, seeing a real opportunity.
S4.quote: I'd be the man they call, and the robots would be my crew.
S4.fieldNote: The decade looks like an opportunity to him rather than a threat, so he stays calm. He admits AGI could run businesses too but trusts village relationships. He worries his crew mates will wait too long and wants to bring them along.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd have no time to save or build anything, and with Hanna's job going too, we'd be in real trouble. What would help is access to small business loans, so people like me can buy the tools and build something, and training for the new robot systems, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the mountains. Up here, everything's harder, weather, roads, logistics. Robots will struggle too, at first. That's my chance. The mountain doesn't care how clever you are, it cares whether you know it.

headlineQuote: The mountain doesn't care how clever you are, it cares whether you know it.
portrait: Ivan Bauer is a 43-year-old lineworker in the mountains who works on towers reached by helicopter and has trialled heavy-lift drones for his company. He preaches at his small church, his wife does bookkeeping for village shops, and with two kids, a mortgage and mountain prices, their savings went on a used truck. He's traditional, free-market and curious, and he uses AI tools every day. He's calm if AI plateaus or changes steadily, anxious about two-year AGI because both incomes would be exposed, and with five or ten years he sees a chance to build his own drone and robot contracting business, which leaves him calm about the slowest picture.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there'd be no time to save or build anything and his wife's job would go too.
whatWouldHelp: Access to small business loans so people like him can buy tools and build something, and training for new robot systems rather than handouts.
